{"file_path":"<path>","content":"# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

If you search text for a living, you already reach for globs (`-g '*.rs'`)
to narrow a search to one kind of file. ripgrep's file-type flags do the
same job, but with a name instead of a pattern you have to remember and
retype. This guide covers the four flags that make up that system:
`--type`/`-t`, `--type-not`/`-T`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## The basic idea: `--type`/`-t`

`--type` limits ripgrep to files matching a named type. A type is just a
name bound to one or more globs. Instead of writing:

```
$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
```

you write:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

or the longer form:

```
$ rg 'int main' --type c
```

`-t` and its type name can be run together (`-trust`) or passed as separate
arguments (`-t rust`, `--type rust`). You can pass `--type` more than once;
each one adds another type to search, so `rg foo -tc -tcpp` searches both C
and C++ files.

Note that `--type` has *lower precedence* than both `-g`/`--glob` and any
rules found in your ignore files. So a `.gitignore` entry or an explicit
`-g '!*.rs'` can still exclude a file even if it matches a type you've
selected.

## Excluding a type: `--type-not`/`-T`

`--type-not` is the mirror image: it excludes files of the given type
rather than including them.

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

Where `-t` means "include files of this type," `-T` means "exclude files
of this type." Like `--type`, `--type-not` can be repeated to exclude
several types at once, and `-t`/`-T` flags can be mixed in the same
invocation — for example `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` excludes Rust and JSON
while including TOML.

## Listing what's available: `--type-list`

Before filtering by a type, it helps to know what it actually matches.
`--type-list` prints every supported type, one per line, as a name
followed by a colon and a comma-separated list of its globs:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types covering well-known
public formats — things like `rust`, `py`/`python`, `markdown`/`md`, `c`,
`cpp`, `go`, and many more (run `--type-list` with no other arguments to
see the full, current set; it changes as new types are added). `--type-list`
also takes into account any `--type-add` or `--type-clear` flags you passed
on the same command line, so it reflects the types actually in effect for
that invocation, not just the built-in defaults.

## Defining your own types: `--type-add`

If none of the built-in types fit, `--type-add` lets you define one. It
takes a single `name:glob` pair, and only one glob per flag — pass
`--type-add` multiple times to add several globs to the same name:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

Brace expansion in the glob lets you do the same thing in one flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

Unless you've used `--type-clear` (below), globs you add with `--type-add`
are added *on top of* any existing globs for that name — including
built-in types. So `--type-add 'rust:*.rspec'` would extend, not replace,
the existing `rust` type.

`--type-add` also supports an `include:` directive, which lets a new type
pull in the rules of other already-defined types by name:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md'
```

This defines `src` as everything matched by the `cpp`, `py`, and `md`
types combined. You can still add more globs to `src` afterward with
another `--type-add`:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
```

Type names may only contain Unicode letters and numbers — no punctuation.

**`--type-add` is not persistent.** It only affects the invocation it's
passed to; ripgrep does not remember custom types between runs. To make a
custom type available every time, either alias the flag into your shell:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` as a line in your ripgrep
configuration file (set via the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment
variable), which ripgrep prepends to every invocation's arguments.

A related flag, `--type-clear TYPE`, removes the globs previously defined
for a type name — including built-in ones — without removing the name
itself, so you can redefine it from scratch with subsequent `--type-add`
flags. Like `--type-add`, it must be passed on every invocation.

## The special `all` type

Both `--type` and `--type-not` accept the special value `all`, which
behaves as if you'd passed the flag once for every type ripgrep knows
about, including any you defined with `--type-add`.

- `--type all` (equivalent to `-t agda -t asciidoc -t asm ...` for every
  known type) puts ripgrep into "whitelist" mode: it searches only files
  it recognizes via *some* type definition.
- `--type-not all` puts it into "blacklist" mode: it searches only files
  that *don't* match any known type.

This distinction matters for files that don't carry a telltale extension.
Suppose your working directory has a shell script `my-shell-script` (no
extension) that sources a library `my-shell-library.bash`. Both
`rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` search `my-shell-library.bash` but skip
`my-shell-script`, because the `sh` type's globs require an extension like
`.bash` or `.sh`. `rg --type-not all`, on the other hand, searches
`my-shell-script` (unrecognized by any type) but skips
`my-shell-library.bash` (recognized).

## Putting it together

A typical workflow: run `rg --type-list` once to check a type's globs or
confirm a name exists, then reach for `-t`/`-T` in day-to-day searches, and
fall back to `--type-add` (aliased or in your config file) when you have a
recurring search over files that don't map cleanly onto a built-in type.
For one-off or highly specific filename patterns, `-g`/`--glob` still wins
on precedence and doesn't require defining a type at all — the two
mechanisms are complementary, not competing.
"}

1	# Filtering by file type in ripgrep
2	
3	If you search text for a living, you already reach for globs (`-g '*.rs'`)
4	to narrow a search to one kind of file. ripgrep's file-type flags do the
5	same job, but with a name instead of a pattern to remember and retype.
6	This guide covers the four flags that make up that system: `--type`/`-t`,
7	`--type-not`/`-T`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.
8	
9	## The basic idea: `--type`/`-t`
10	
11	`--type` limits ripgrep to files matching a named type. A type is just a
12	name bound to one or more globs. Instead of writing:
13	
14	```
15	$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
16	```
17	
18	you write:
19	
20	```
21	$ rg 'int main' -tc
22	```
23	
24	or the longer form:
25	
26	```
27	$ rg 'int main' --type c
28	```
29	
30	`-t` and its type name can be run together (`-trust`) or passed as separate
31	arguments (`-t rust`, `--type rust`). You can pass `--type` more than once;
32	each one adds another type to search, so `rg foo -tc -tcpp` searches both C
33	and C++ files.
34	
35	Note that `--type` has *lower precedence* than both `-g`/`--glob` and any
36	rules found in your ignore files. A `.gitignore` entry or an explicit
37	`-g '!*.rs'` can still exclude a file even if it matches a type you've
38	selected.
39	
40	## Excluding a type: `--type-not`/`-T`
41	
42	`--type-not` is the mirror image: it excludes files of the given type
43	rather than including them.
44	
45	```
46	$ rg clap --type-not rust
47	$ rg clap -Trust
48	```
49	
50	Where `-t` means "include files of this type," `-T` means "exclude files
51	of this type." Like `--type`, `--type-not` can be repeated to exclude
52	several types at once, and `-t`/`-T` flags can be mixed in the same
53	invocation — for example `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` excludes Rust and JSON
54	while including TOML.
55	
56	## Listing what's available: `--type-list`
57	
58	Before filtering by a type, it helps to know what it actually matches.
59	`--type-list` prints every supported type, one per line, as a name
60	followed by a colon and a comma-separated list of its globs:
61	
62	```
63	$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
64	make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
65	```
66	
67	ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types covering well-known
68	public formats — things like `rust`, `py`/`python`, `markdown`/`md`, `c`,
69	`cpp`, and `go` (run `--type-list` with no other arguments for the full,
70	current set). `--type-list` also takes into account any `--type-add` or
71	`--type-clear` flags on the same command line, so it reflects the types
72	actually in effect for that invocation, not just the built-in defaults.
73	
74	## Defining your own types: `--type-add`
75	
76	If none of the built-in types fit, `--type-add` lets you define one. It
77	takes a single `name:glob` pair, and only one glob per flag — pass
78	`--type-add` multiple times to add several globs to the same name:
79	
80	```
81	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
82	```
83	
84	Brace expansion in the glob lets you do the same thing in one flag:
85	
86	```
87	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
88	```
89	
90	Unless you've used `--type-clear` (below), globs added with `--type-add`
91	go *on top of* any existing globs for that name — including built-in
92	types. So `--type-add 'rust:*.rspec'` extends, rather than replaces, the
93	existing `rust` type.
94	
95	`--type-add` also supports an `include:` directive, which lets a new type
96	pull in the rules of other already-defined types by name:
97	
98	```
99	$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md'
100	```
101	
102	This defines `src` as everything matched by the `cpp`, `py`, and `md`
103	types combined. You can still add more globs to `src` afterward with
104	another `--type-add`:
105	
106	```
107	$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
108	```
109	
110	Type names may only contain Unicode letters and numbers — no punctuation.
111	
112	**`--type-add` is not persistent.** It only affects the invocation it's
113	passed to; ripgrep does not remember custom types between runs. To make a
114	custom type available every time, either alias the flag into your shell:
115	
116	```
117	alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
118	```
119	
120	or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` as a line in your ripgrep
121	configuration file (set via the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment
122	variable), which ripgrep prepends to every invocation's arguments.
123	
124	A related flag, `--type-clear TYPE`, removes the globs previously defined
125	for a type name — including built-in ones — without removing the name
126	itself, so you can redefine it from scratch with subsequent `--type-add`
127	flags. Like `--type-add`, it must be passed on every invocation.
128	
129	## The special `all` type
130	
131	Both `--type` and `--type-not` accept the special value `all`, which
132	behaves as if you'd passed the flag once for every type ripgrep knows
133	about, including any you defined with `--type-add`.
134	
135	- `--type all` (equivalent to `-t agda -t asciidoc -t asm ...` for every
136	  known type) puts ripgrep into "whitelist" mode: it searches only files
137	  it recognizes via *some* type definition.
138	- `--type-not all` puts it into "blacklist" mode: it searches only files
139	  that *don't* match any known type.
140	
141	This distinction matters for files that don't carry a telltale extension.
142	Suppose your working directory has a shell script `my-shell-script` (no
143	extension) that sources a library `my-shell-library.bash`. Both
144	`rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` search `my-shell-library.bash` but skip
145	`my-shell-script`, because the `sh` type's globs require an extension like
146	`.bash` or `.sh`. `rg --type-not all`, on the other hand, searches
147	`my-shell-script` (unrecognized by any type) but skips
148	`my-shell-library.bash` (recognized).
149	
150	## Putting it together
151	
152	A typical workflow: run `rg --type-list` once to check a type's globs or
153	confirm a name exists, reach for `-t`/`-T` in day-to-day searches, and fall
154	back to `--type-add` (aliased or in your config file) for a recurring
155	search over files that don't map onto a built-in type. For one-off or
156	highly specific filename patterns, `-g`/`--glob` still wins on precedence
157	and needs no type definition — the two mechanisms complement each other.
158
